rationale: The title and abstract examine post-civil-war rural land governance reforms, legalisation of communal customary land rights, local state-building, and ethnic conflict over territory in South Sudan. There is no mention or examination of household or community water or sanitation services or service-access outcomes (E01: wrong topic).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Excluded under both narrow and plain readings of Criterion 2 because the study is entirely off-topic (rural land governance, state-building, and ethnic conflict in South Sudan) with no household or community water or sanitation service access component (E01).

evidence_quotes.quote: Building a Fragmented State: Land Governance and Conflict in South Sudan
Communal customary rights to land have been legalised to reduce rural people's economic vulnerability and satisfy one of the major grievances that led to war.
To date this has appeared to strengthen ethnic affiliation as a means to access resources and enrich government officers' repertoires for claiming control over the territory
